Hisn will send DNS requests through Cloudflare Families to block matching domains. Cloudflare can see these requests. Hisn keeps no browsing log. Android allows one VPN, so another VPN may disconnect. You can turn this off in Hisn.

Hisn checks supported IPv4 UDP and TCP DNS requests to its virtual DNS server against the bundled list and your saved rules. Allowed requests go to Cloudflare Families (1.1.1.3, or its second address 1.0.0.3 when 1.1.1.3 cannot be reached) over authenticated, encrypted DNS-over-TLS. Cloudflare can see these requests. Hisn does not save a browsing log or fall back to plaintext DNS.

Android allows one VPN per profile. Starting Hisn can disconnect your existing VPN.

Hisn answers well-known encrypted-DNS provider names and Firefox’s DNS-over-HTTPS canary domain with “not found”. This reduces, but does not stop, apps using their own encrypted DNS: some reach providers at built-in IP addresses. This DNS layer also does not cover direct IP access, cached answers, images or videos. Optional visual checks are a separate layer. TCP is bounded to DNS port 53 and messages up to 4096 bytes; unsupported requests or resolver failures can interrupt loading. Client TLS on port 853 is refused so Android uses port 53 instead. Hisn also routes the fixed addresses of well-known public encrypted-DNS resolvers into its tunnel and drops them, so an app that hard-codes one of those addresses cannot use it to bypass filtering. Other providers, app-specific resolvers and shared CDN addresses are not covered. If Android Private DNS is set to a provider hostname, system DNS can bypass Hisn; Hisn warns but does not change that setting. This is a DNS-only tunnel and does not enable VPN lockdown. On a device-owner phone with managed lockdown on, Hisn can ask Android to keep this tunnel always on while DNS filtering is on; Android’s own VPN settings may also offer always-on. If you leave DNS filtering on, Hisn starts it again after a restart while Android still holds this VPN approval. You can disconnect through Android VPN settings.

Sensitive content may still appear elsewhere, including in a field of a window you have moved away from. Select only apps you want captured.

While a selected app has a window on screen, a sample is requested about every two seconds: about every second while it scrolls or changes, and up to every five seconds while the screen stays still. One window is sampled at a time, with one request at a time; several selected windows take turns. Nothing is sampled while the screen is off. Flagged samples return you to Home with a restriction notice, or close a flagged picture-in-picture window where Android allows it. This restricts the whole app screen; it does not blur individual images or pause individual videos. The separate Blur people setting can cover the whole screen when a face matches your chosen group; that is an appearance estimate, not identity, and it can hide the wrong faces. Content can appear before intervention. Small images, short video frames and classification mistakes leave gaps. A protected or private window that blocks screenshots is covered rather than inspected. Unknown samples are not marked clean. Android 14+ is required.

While it runs, the app also arms the direct build’s removal guard even if its switch is off, and a device owner gets Android’s uninstall block. The direct guard closes Hisn’s uninstall and disable screens and the Safe Mode prompt; boot-key Safe Mode, ADB, root and a factory reset still remove Hisn, and the Play build cannot block an uninstall at all.

Lock time counts while the device is running, including after a restart. Time while the device is switched off is not counted, so powering off extends the period; Hisn does not trust a changed date. Daily schedules instead follow the device clock and time zone, which can still be changed outside Hisn.

1. In Rules, choose blocked apps, a daily schedule, or apps to inspect. Built-in adult-text and image/video checks are separate optional layers.

2. Review the accessibility disclosure and enable Hisn in Android settings for app restrictions or inspections. Image/video checks need Android 14+.

3. In Protection, review DNS filtering and approve the Android VPN request for domain blocking. Another VPN may disconnect.

4. Run the DNS route check and review each layer’s status. A passed check verifies only that DNS path.

Where the bundled lists and engine come from

Hisn includes data and code from other projects. Their licenses apply to those parts. The full license texts are listed after this summary; they are stored in the app and nothing is downloaded.

Bundled domain list: Hisn builds it from these adult sources, then filters and merges them:
• StevenBlack hosts: the porn-only list (github.com/StevenBlack/hosts), MIT License
• Sinfonietta hostfiles: the pornography list (github.com/Sinfonietta/hostfiles), MIT License
• HaGeZi DNS blocklists: the NSFW list (github.com/hagezi/dns-blocklists), GNU GPL 3.0
• chadmayfield Pi-hole blocklists: adult domains among the top one million sites (github.com/chadmayfield/my-pihole-blocklists), GNU GPL 3.0
• The Block List Project: the pornography list (github.com/blocklistproject/Lists), Unlicense
• oisd: the NSFW list (oisd.nl), free for personal and commercial use

A selected subset of the last two is bundled only where both lists agree and the domain carries an adult signal. The full Mac and network list also uses a saved snapshot of the unified hosts list, which is not in this APK.

The list is a plain-text file inside the app (domains_core.txt). The scripts that build it are in the Hisn source repository.

Word list: some German terms in the bundled vocabulary come from the List of Dirty, Naughty, Obscene, and Otherwise Bad Words by its LDNOOBW contributors (github.com/LDNOOBW), Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. Hisn kept only terms that also appear in adult domain names and set its own weights.

Image-check engine: the bundled TensorFlow.js, NSFWJS, Human, MediaPipe and other code and models keep the notices listed after this summary, including the engine’s full third-party license file.

resources.string: Only a device owner can make Android refuse to uninstall an app. Hisn applies that while a protection lock runs or while you choose to keep it installed. The direct build also closes its removal screens while a lock runs, even when its switch is off. This is separate from the ordinary Play build, which cannot block uninstall.

Managed mode requires provisioning device ownership outside Hisn, usually on a factory-reset device with no accounts. It is intended for a phone you control, not for concealing the app. After the protection lock and the keep-installed choice are both off, the app offers a release action so Android can remove it again.

This is broader than keeping Hisn installed: it stops uninstalling, disabling, force-stopping or clearing the data of every app, blocks Safe Mode, the Settings erase and adding users, and prevents manual date and time changes on Android 9 and later, changing default apps on Android 14 and later, VPN configuration changes and, on Android 10 and later, Private DNS changes. It is available only while Hisn is this phone’s device owner, applies while a protection lock or Keep Hisn installed is active, and can be turned off when no protection lock runs. When DNS filtering is on, it also asks Android to keep the DNS-only tunnel always on, so another VPN cannot be used while DNS filtering is on. Recovery mode, ADB and removing device ownership still override it.

Message or call someone you trust, even just to say hello.

This direct build uses accessibility to close the screens that would remove or switch off Hisn: the uninstall confirmation, Hisn’s App info page (force stop, clear data), device-admin deactivation, Hisn’s accessibility toggle, and the power menu’s Safe Mode prompt. When it closes one, a full-screen protection page explains what happened and holds the ways forward for a few seconds. Power off and restart still work, and other Settings pages stay usable.

A running protection lock turns this guard on automatically, even when the keep-installed switch is off. The install-only switch is separate and also stops a new app’s install confirmation and a Play Store page that offers Install, so another browser or VPN cannot be installed from those screens. It works only while Hisn’s accessibility service is on. Starting Safe Mode with the hardware keys at boot, ADB, root or a factory reset still remove Hisn; only device-owner mode makes Android itself refuse an uninstall. During a protection lock you cannot turn these off.

Hisn uses Android accessibility to identify selected apps and inspect their visible text. If you separately enable image/video checks, Hisn also takes transient screenshots of selected app windows; review that option’s separate disclosure in Rules. Your app restrictions, daily schedule or matching words can return you to the home screen and show a restriction notice.

In this direct build, if you turn on either screen-guard switch or start a protection lock, Hisn also reads the visible text of Settings, the package installer and Play Store windows to recognise Hisn’s own uninstall, App info, device-admin and accessibility screens and a new app’s Install confirmation, and of System UI windows (the power menu, which shares System UI with the notification shade) to recognise the Safe Mode prompt. It closes those screens and then shows the protection page.

Text is processed on this device and is not saved or sent to a server. Input fields, password fields and their child elements are skipped where Android identifies them. Some sensitive text may still appear in ordinary labels or messages. Select only apps you want inspected.

What Hisn does and where it stops

Choose apps and one daily foreground-time limit. When the limit is reached, Hisn closes the app and returns you home until local midnight. Hisn reads Android’s own on-device usage record; no usage event leaves the phone.

Requires Hisn accessibility to be connected and the separate Android Usage access grant. Android’s foreground-time record resets at local midnight; it can differ slightly from what you experienced, and changing the device clock, time zone or date or clearing Android’s usage data can change it. Limits are checked when a selected app is on screen and about once a minute while it stays there, so a limit may be enforced a little late. Settings, dialers, launchers and Hisn are excluded. While a protection lock runs, every saved limit is read-only.
